CAMP TRAINERS 
AND

Sturdy, Stable

SPRITE 

The "Sprite is well named for she is the perfect 
boat to start the younger set in sailing. She rep¬ 
resents unusual value because it is the only boat of 
its kind with such a wonderful combination of features 
—lively sailing ability, stability and safety, fiberglass 
construction and convertible rig. 

The Sprite gives the beginner a wide range of 
sailboat “feeling". She can be rigged with a single 
sail as a catboat, or with a mainsail and jib as a 
sloop; and she also flys a spinnaker to provide 
training in the important and exciting downwind 
sailing. 

SPECIFICATIONS 

Length: 10', width (beam) 4'4"; freeboard 17"; sail 
area; main—53.2 sq. ft., 16.2 sq. ft.; weight 150 
lbs. (approx.); wood mast and boom, aluminum 
pivoting rudder and centerboard; seat 1 to 3; stan¬ 
dard colors molded in; dacron sails. 

Specifications subject to change without notice. 

OTTER PRAM 

Combining the proven pram configuration, with a 
durable and strong fiberglass construction, the vers¬ 
atile O'Day Otter offers an ideal solution to many 
requirements. Both rowing and sailing models make 
excellent tenders; light for easy handling on davits 
or for hauling onto cabin tops. The Otter, with 
built in buoyancy for safety, is a barrel of fun for 
children, whether at a cottage, yacht club or quiet 
anchorage on a cruise. They provide ample capacity 
for adults when fishing, transferring gear and supplies 
to and from a yacht, having a morning constitutional 
row or a relaxing evening sail. 

If you have ever owned a plywood pram, you 
have likely had the discouraging experience of 
constant maintenance. An Otter will last almost 
indefinitly, and only an occasional scrubbing is neces¬ 
sary to freshen its appearance. 

For any small boat purpose you may wish, the 
O'Day Otter stands second to none. The low cost, 
dependable service, and long life of an Otter, make 
it a very worthwhile asset to any boating family. 

SPECIFICATIONS 

Length 7'9"; Beam 4'1" ; Depth 14%"; Weight 74 lbs. 
Sailing Model—Draff 2'4"; Dacron Sail, 35 square 
feet. 


BEAVER 

She’s perfect for an instructor to teach two or 
even four youngsters at a time. Youngsters learn how 
to handle her sloop rig and its parachute—and to 
really teach the details, the why and hows of a main, 
jib and spinnaker plus the proper balancing of a 
centerboard boat—the Beaver is tops. 

SAFETY . . . The Beaver is almost impossible to 
tip over even with sheets tied in heavy air and 
through many jibes. The Beaver has built in flotation 
tanks, doubling as seats along both sides, plus a bow 
tank which will support the boat and crew if 
swamped, and makes it possible to "bail and sail" 
away. 

FIBERGLASS CONSTRUCTION . . . One of the 
most important features of the Beaver is her mainten¬ 
ance-free one piece Fiberglass hull which is unusually 
strong, will not leak or corrode. 

SPECIFICATIONS 

Length 14', Beam 6'. Draft—CB up 9", CB down 4'. 
Sail area (main and jib) 107 sq. ft. Freeboard 
midships 16". Mast and Boom (Aluminum) Aluminum 
centreboard, bronze fittings, built-in buoyancy tanks, 
dacron sails. 


HALADNER CANOE 

Traditional design in modern materials 
The ideal camp canoe, for long service. In the 
beautiful Haladner canoe you will find all of the 
proved features of traditional design — and more. 
Years of experience in summer camp management in 
which canoeing played a major part led to the 
selection of the Haladner design. It took three more 
years to reproduce it in smooth, durable, ever 
gleaming glass fiber. 

SPECIFICATIONS 

Length 16'; Width 33"; Depth at centre 12"; Weight 
72 pounds, with perfect balance for easy portaging.

LEADERSHIP 

by Hedley G. Dimock, 

Centre for Human Relations 
and Community Studies, 

Sir George Williams University, Montreal 


A Major Dimension 
in Camp Effectiveness 


As presented at the 7th Annual Camp Directors 9 Seminar, 
Alberta Camping Association, Feb. 5-8 1964 


Groups are a powerful force in 
developing an individual’s social skill 
and determining his success and hap¬ 
piness in life. Through the group ex¬ 
perience that camps offer, an individual 
may meet many of his psychological 
needs, develop behaviour skills which 
contribute to his good mental health, 
learn social skills including those of 
democratic decision making, and ac¬ 
quire the norms and customs of his 
society. Through group membership 
some modification of his behaviour and 
attitudes will take place. As an indi¬ 
vidual tries out various forms of be¬ 
haviour in his group he is able to work, 
out an accurate and realistic concept 
of himself and develop the flexible be¬ 
haviour that will result in a well- 
adjusted person who is successful in his 
relations with others. A major dimen¬ 
sion affecting the growth of the group 
and its influence on the members is 
the leadership provided by the 
counsellor. 

Nearly everyone in camping has ideas 
about what the characteristics of suc¬ 
cessful counsellors are and how these 
counsellors can be motivated to do 
their best work. In the past twenty 
years, research in camping and the 
social sciences has shed a great deal of 
light on qualities of effective leadership 
and the conditions encouraging the full 
use of leadership potential. 

It is popular belief that a person is 
a successful leader because of certain 


personality traits or leadership qualities 
which he has and which other 
people do not have. Some people be¬ 
lieve that these men are born with 
qualities for great leadership and will 
be leaders regardless of what enterprises 
they undertake. Hence, it used to be a 
common practice for camps to take 
campus or athletic leaders to camp with 
the expectation that they would be 
successful staff. 

The early studies of leadership there¬ 
fore attempted to identify the character¬ 
istics of leaders. If these characteristics 
could be identified, then real leaders 
could be singled out and put to work im¬ 
proving the productivity of groups. The 
studies of the personality of leaders 
have been disappointing as they have 
failed to find any consistent pattern 
which distinguishes leaders from 
non-leaders. This research led to the 
conclusion that leaders do not have 
particular personalities or traits, identi¬ 
fiable at this time, that separate them 
from other people. The “leaders are 
born” theory of leadership has been 
abandoned because of lack of scien¬ 
tific support. The theory most widely 
accepted by social scientists sees leader¬ 
ship as a function of the situation as 
it interacts with the personalities of the 
members, and their needs or tasks. 
Leaders have certain personality traits 
that likely increase the probability of 
their taking on leadership functions, 
but their success as a leader is largely 
dependent upon the situation. 


94 


Canadian Camping 


A person who is a leader in one 
situation may not be a leader in an¬ 
other, and a person who gives leader¬ 
ship to one group may not be a leader 
in a different group. Joe may be the 
person in the group most able to lead 
them on a hike, but Bill is the most 
able to organize a skit night. The 
campus athlete may be scared of the 
woods or find it hard to be patient 
with rowdy ten-year-olds. 

During the second world war the 
O.S.S. ran an extensive programme to 
help them locate potential undercover 
agents for espionage work, and since 
the war the U.S. Navy has carried out 
numerous leadership studies at Ohio 
State University and elsewhere. These 
studies have supported the conclusion 
that people who are leaders in one 
situation may not be leaders in another. 
Although there are certain character¬ 
istics and behaviour patterns that enable 
a person to take leadership more suc¬ 
cessfully, these in themselves are no 
guarantee of leadership. Those who 
give leadership in one situation may or 
may not give leadership in another 
but, in any case, their leadership po¬ 
tential is more related to their social 
experiences than to the characteristics 
with which they were born. 

Leadership is best defined as “doing 
something that helps solve a problem 
or accomplish an objective.” A group’s 
objective may be the achievement of 
some specific goal (task) or maintain¬ 
ing and developing itself as a group 
(group building). The counsellor or 
campers perform leadership functions 
by helping the group in one or both 
of these two areas; however, some 
individuals who do not contribute task 
or group building functions may also 
influence the behaviour of the group. 
If such an individual is well accepted 
by the group or the group is in an 
excited state, his behaviour may be 
contagious. The situation in which a 
group finds itself determines to some 


extent what leadership acts will be 
needed at any given time and who 
among the members will perform them. 
Any member who helps the group 
achieve its goals, or influences the be¬ 
haviour of the group, is a “leader”. 
Most members are leaders of the group 
at one time or another, hence, we must 
study a corps of leaders and differen¬ 
tiate among members according to the 
amount of leadership they contribute 
to the group. In some groups the 
organization and structure may be such 
that members expect one person to 
give leadership and he may, therefore, 
stand head and shoulders above the 
others as leader. For our purpose, we 
should think of leaders as those mem¬ 
bers in a specific group situation who 
provide a large share of the leadership 
acts. 

Some Characteristics of Leaders 

Every individual of a group is more 
or less a leader in that he affects the 
behaviour of the group, but some indi¬ 
viduals tend to lead more frequently 
than others. Research has turned up 
some characteristics which may make 
certain individuals especially prone to 
giving leadership to a group, and these 
are the ones camps want as counsellors. 

In youth groups, physical size has 
some relation to leadership potential, 
and it is likely that this is related to 
athletic success where size is an im¬ 
portant factor. In adult groups, size 
(height or weight) does not appear 
related to leadership acts. Members 
most active in leadership roles generally 
have more energy (and likely better 
physical health), and are more tidy 
and attractive in appearance than the 
other members of the group. “Leaders” 
usually have slightly greater personal 
capacity such as intelligence, insight, 
fluency of speech, initiative, ambition, 
soundness of judgment and originality. 

In an extensive study of high school 
basketball teams and several other adult 
turn to page 126 


Toronto , Canada , April 1964 


*95 



Teamwork and 


Staff Relations 


by W . ]. Eastaugh, 

Assistant Director, Camp Ahmek . 


If the remarks in this article appear 
at times to stray from the subject 
“Teamwork and Staff Relations” 
blame it on bias. This topic encom¬ 
passes such a wide range of camping 
that it has proven difficult to narrow 
the discussion. It is inconceivable to¬ 
day that a director of a dynamic enter¬ 
prise like a camp would operate with¬ 
out involving the staff in the areas pre¬ 
sented here. If the campers are to par¬ 
ticipate in a programme designed to 
foster mental, physical and spiritual 
growth, they must be led by a staff 
trained and knowledgeable in the con¬ 
cepts and processes which will provide 
an atmosphere in which these goals 
may be realized. Unless the director of 
the camp challenges the staff to parti¬ 
cipate in the development of policies 
and practices necessary to create such 
a climate, the basic aims of the camp 
will go unrealized. The camp director 
knows what the goals are, but if the 
staff is to adopt them they must have 
an opportunity to examine and under¬ 
stand them. The camp director be¬ 
lieves the staff is capable of leading 
the campers. He must also believe they 
are capable of and interested in devel¬ 
oping the means of achieving the best 
results. He doesn’t compromise. He 
accepts the total responsibility for the 
actions of his staff. He can do this 
because he has faith in the staff he has 
selected. It is this solid, unwavering 
confidence in the ability of the group 
to reach the best solution to problems 
related to the camp programme that is 
the basis of teamwork and staff morale. 


He must work at making his camp a 
vital experience year after year, if he 
wishes to protect his investment. 

No aspect of camping is more vital 
to success than that of staff relation¬ 
ship and teamwork. I suppose every 
director tells his staff that camp is for 
the campers. This is true but he should 
honestly admit that it is also for the 
staff—and then make sure that the 
needs of both are met. Happily both 
groups can enjoy camp simultaneously; 
but it follows as surely as night the day 
that if the staff is edgy, unco-opera¬ 
tive, ill-informed, suspicious or incom¬ 
petent, the campers will not have a 
happy summer. They may return once 
but unless corrective measures are in¬ 
troduced, repeat enrolments will 
diminish. 

Having fun is a rightful expectation 
of the staff. Few camps can afford to 
pay for services in cash—part of the 
remuneration must come from the sat¬ 
isfactions inherent in being a part of 
a successful team engaged in a dy¬ 
namic undertaking. 

Frank Discussion 

The subject of pay and finances is 
an important one. The director selects 
his staff on the basis of maturity and 
common sense. Might it not serve as 
a means of establishing a basis for 
frankness if the camp books were to 
be opened for inspection? How much 
harm would it do for the staff of 
agency camps to know what it costs to 
operate for the period under question? 


96 


Canadian Camping 



Most private camp owners might be 
pleasantly surprised at the added rap¬ 
port that would develop when his staff 
realized that their estimate of profit 
(for they do calculate) was far in ex¬ 
cess of reality. Such a move could pave 
the way for a dramatic presentation of 
the importance of the counsellor’s job 
as measured in dollars and cents. Not 
that monetary considerations are to 
form the basis of staff relations—sim¬ 
ply a possible approach that may be 
worth exploring. 

There is just one more monetary 
matter for our consideration. The 
camp policy regarding salaries should 
be available for staff to examine and 
it should be possible to defend. The 
camp director who believes he can 
prevent his staff from discussing sal¬ 
aries is unrealistic. All camps should, 
and I believe do, pay what their opera¬ 
tion can afford and therefore the cal¬ 
culations which are used to arrive at 
this amount can often be used as the 
answer to any criticism. Staff have a 
right to question the fairness of paying 
more for the services of a person whose 
experience, duties, age and skills are 
the same as one who is paid less. An 
increase in pay for the second or third 
summer is a reasonable expectation 
and should result in a higher rate than 
a beginner. 

Choosing Staff 

The selection of staff is an import¬ 
ant element in teamwork. Here again 
a policy needs to be established, a 
policy that will be understood by the 
staff and acceptable to them. A camp 
that includes in its objectives elements 
of leadership training and character 
development should naturally provide 
opportunities for campers to join the 
staff when they reach the required age 
and maturity. To deny this oppor¬ 
tunity, or to neglect to encourage 
young campers to aspire to staff status, 
is tantamount to condemning the 


quality of the camp programme. When 
an organization begins to draw its 
leaders from its own developmental 
programme it demonstrates that it has 
the courage of its convictions. These 
are people the director knows. He has 
seen them grow and he has a personal 
interest and investment in their future. 
This is his reward—many times more 
valuable than wealth and much more 
satisfying. 

But there is little chance that all 
staff requirements will come from this 
source, and really little to recommend 
it. Good staff people are gems and just 
as rare. All too often they are rough 
and unpolished. They await the pa¬ 
tient, skillful shaping of a master gem- 
ologist—the camp director. The liter¬ 
ature is full of suggestions for selecting 
the right personnel but nowhere is 
there a foolproof method of locating 
helpers to suit the personality of a par¬ 
ticular director or a particular camp. 
Money will not buy nor hold key 
people. Friendship, genuine and sin¬ 
cere, will. Apart from the weak sis¬ 
ters which are weeded out, a certain 
turnover in staff is inevitable. Young 
people embark on careers; some relin¬ 
quish ties with camp; in other instances 
the association has been retained due 
to special arrangements. 

What to do about the return of a 
valued ex-staffer poses a problem. 
Since experienced help is always an 
asset, most camp directors welcome 
such people. But what does this do for 
the current crop of eager beavers? It 
seems to me that the only fair and safe 
way to re-engage these ex-staffers is in 
some capacity other than their original 
jobs if they are already being filled. 
Staff friction could be detrimental and 
offset the advantages of having the old 
staffer back. 

FriendsMns play an important part 
in staff relations and in retaining staff,

Retrospectives sur la Centeriare - Voyageurs de Passe 

Canadian Centenary Journey 

****** 

At the request of the Canadian Citizens’ Centenary Committee, a committee within the 
Canadian Camping Association was formed to explore the possibilities of undertaking a 
centenary project in the form of a Cross-Canada Canoe Trip. They presented their 
recommendations to the C.C.A. Annual Meeting in 1963 at which time they were asked 
to continue this study. The results of their deliberations have been presented at this year’s 
Annual Meeting in the form of the following proposal which was enthusiastically endorsed 
at the meeting. Provincial associations are now forming their committees to share in the 
planning and carrying forward of the project. If you will lend your support, please get in 
touch with your provincial association. 

* * * * 


The first explorers, who charted the 
coasts of what are now Canada’s mari¬ 
time provinces and sailed up the St. 
Lawrence River, were deeply impressed 
by the quality and profusion of the 
fur-bearing animals that provided the 
Indians with food and clothing. 

The European demand for fur being 
what it was, a flourishing trade in 
beaver pelts developed early in the 
seventeenth century, and helped lay the 
economic foundation of Canada. 

At first, Indian trappers brought their 
furs to posts at Quebec and other 
pioneer settlements for trade. Some 
even acted as middlemen for distant 
tribes eager to exchange their pelts for 
knives, blankets and muskets. These 
Indians traversed the wilderness water¬ 
ways in the craft they had perfected 
for the purpose: the birchbark canoe. 

However, by the middle of the seven¬ 
teenth century, the more adventurous 
Europeans — men of the stamp of 
Champlain, Dulhut, LaSalle and Le- 
Verendrye—were pushing rapidly into 
the interior of the continent, searching 
for routes to the Orient and enlarging 
the scope of the fur trade. Like the 
Indians, they travelled in canoes, and 
made use of the wonderful system of 
waterways that led from the coasts to 
the heart of the strange new land. 


Fortunately, though two centuries 
and more have passed, many of these 
water routes are still open and navig¬ 
able. Where civilization has not en¬ 
croached, ancient portages and camp 
sites are still in use, as well as shortcuts 
developed through trial-and-error by 
Indians and voyageurs. 

Because of the importance in Can¬ 
adian history , therefore , and because 
they are still open for use and enjoy¬ 
ment, the Canadian Camping Associa¬ 
tion would like to consider these 
waterways in terms of a Centenary 
Project. 

Such a project would consist of three 
major elements: 

First, a programme of mapping the 
routes in their entirety in every 
province. 

Second, a co-ordinated canoeing pro¬ 
gramme, whereby organized groups of 
Association members would paddle and 
portage along these routes, each group 
within its own province. 

Third, a campaign of publicising 
these first two elements in such a 
manner that Canadians, and visitors to 
Canada, will become aware of our his¬ 
toric water routes, and will learn how 

turn to page 124 


98 


Canadian Camping 



Counsellors can Help 


by Elsie K. Palter, 
Camp Kawagama 


Their Campers 


From her presentation on “Behaviour Problems at Camp” at the Ontario Camping 
Association Conference, March 1963. 


We, who are in camping, are very 
fortunate people. We enjoy the privi¬ 
lege of observing and contributing to 
the growth and development of the 
youngsters in our care through the ex¬ 
periences they have in our camps. And 
probably there is nothing more reward¬ 
ing in all this than to realize that they 
have been better able to meet difficulties 
and shoulder their particular burdens 
in life because of their life with us at 
camp. 

Any group of children ready for 
departure for camp give some evidence 
of their expectations; some look eager 
and joyful, others withdrawn and sub¬ 
dued and maybe even frightened. For 
many weeks and even months, parents 
and campers have been getting ready 
for this experience—buying and (we 
hope) marking clothes and sports 
equipment. In addition to these posses¬ 
sions, our campers bring with them 
other things which are not so obvious, 
for which we are not always prepared, 
and which they themselves may not 
realize they have. I refer to those 
“things” which come from their family 
backgrounds, from their own experi¬ 
ences. Some come laden down with 
parental expectations— they have been 
told they must learn to swim, to play 
the games, to take care of their personal 
belongings, to get along with others. 


These burdens can make them anxious 
and worried if they do not succeed. 
These are burdens for us too. In addi¬ 
tion, the child brings his own burdens, 
which may also be family engendered. 
He may bring a need to be outstanding 
like his brother. In our society today, 
with emphasis on competition. Little 
Leagues, high grades in school, ad¬ 
mission to college—our children have 
some real concerns and burdens. 

A youngster’s basic attitudes and 
values, and point of view, and his 
ways of reacting are so much influenced 
by the experiences he has had in his 
home, that we must be constantly 
aware of this factor. When he comes to 
camp, we recognize that camp is a 
different experience for a child than is 
the home experience, and this is as it 
should be. In our culture, children 
need to grow out, to grow away or 
develop more and wider experiences 
and contacts. Camp life affords this 
opportunity. We know he needs other 
kinds of relationships with adults as 
well as the parent-child relationship. 
We must be ready to help the child 
bridge the change from home to camp. 
Leadership at camp must be warm, 
understanding, dependable and sym¬ 
pathetic; never domineering, authori¬ 
tative and nagging. 

♦ 


Toronto, Canada, April 1964 


99 





In order to understand behaviour , 
let us pause very briefly to consider the 
Basic Needs by which behaviour is 
determined. These needs have been 
listed by numerous psychologists. Here 
is A. H. Maslow’s list, in order from 
lowest to highest needs: 

1. Physiological needs such as hunger, 
thirst, activity, rest, etc. 

2. Safety needs, security, and release 
from anxiety aroused by threat of 
various kinds. 

3. Love needs including love, affection, 
acceptance and feeling of belonging 
in one’s relationships with parents, 
teachers, friends and other social 
groups. 

4. Esteem needs including both self¬ 
esteem from mastery and confidence 
in one’s own worth, adequacy, and 
capacities, and the esteem from 
social approval. 

5. Need for self-actualization through 
creative self-expression in personal 
and social achievements; need to 
feel free to act (within the limits of 
general social needs), to satisfy one’s 
curiosity, and to understand one’s 
world. 

The first four needs here are to a 
certain extent self-centered. Only when 
lower order needs are satisfied can 
higher order needs determine be¬ 
haviour. “A child who is hungry, in¬ 
secure, or unloved, whose confidence 
has been undermined by failures, or 
who feels disapproved would not be ex¬ 
pected to reach this fifth level level; 
consequently he would not be expected 
to devote his efforts constructively and 
creatively to his school tasks and pro¬ 
jects. All his energies would be mobil¬ 
ized in his efforts to allay hunger, or 
to relieve anxiety, or to win love or 
esteem (but not necessarily by con¬ 
structive effort).” Research has revealed 
that love is beyond all question the 
most important experience in the life 
of a human being. 


Let us now consider the children 
who come to spend their holidays with 
us and what we observe about them 
here. Camp offers a new setting for 
children and often in one season or 
over several seasons some problems 
they are facing can be overcome and 
new goals and directions achieved by 
child. The counsellor, who has been 
carefully selected for his job, because 
of his objectivity can achieve a re¬ 
lationship which the campers’ parents 
fail to attain. Sometimes the change 
from home environment to a new situ¬ 
ation provides the incentive for more 
responsible behaviour. Sometimes the 
close relationships between camper and 
other campers have a strong impact 
and serve as the motivating factor. 
Often, a youngster finds a relationship 
with some adult in the camp other 
than his own counsellor whom he 
respects and to whom he relates so well 
that this serves as his inspiration. 

The atmosphere of camp, in a rec¬ 
reational setting, geared to the fun 
and pleasure of the camper, helps to 
relax the child and may make him 
happier and change his attitude. The 
acquisition of skills, success in some 
aspect of the programme, add to his 
self-esteem and self-confidence. The 
total broadening experience of camp, 
its social contacts with different people, 
better understanding of one’s self, all 
add to the effectiveness of a camp 
experience. 

Because we are dealing with human 
beings, and there are no perfect 
campers, we must be ready to accept 
the children who come into our care. 
The adjustment of children at camp 
varies—some defy discipline, some show 
off, some steal and some withdraw. 
Our concern here is with some of the 
normal problems which we meet as 
counsellors. Problem campers need

ARE YOU TRAINING 



YOUR STAFF 


With Health 
and Safety 
in Mind? 


by Joy M. Ballard , B.A.-M.D. 
Camp Brigadoon 


Responsibility for the health and 
safety of children at camp rests on 
the shoulders of the parents, the 
camp director, camp doctor and nurse, 
on the campers themselves to a certain 
extent, but to a greater extent on the 
counsellors. Ideally all will co-operate 
fully : but careful thought must be given 
by the director to this most vital aspect 
of camp life, with time set aside during 
pre-camp to discuss health and safety 
standards and the reasons for their 
being. 

In view of the fact that counsellors 
are in closest contact with campers, 
their role in the maintenance of health 
cannot be over-emphasized. It is up to 
the director, working with the medical 
staff, to train counsellors to be ever on 
the alert, to watch for and report: 
fatigue, rashes, pallor, loss of appetite, 
coughs, sneezes and sniffles, lassitude, 
irritability, depression, drowsiness or 
insomnia. 

Foremost in importance to the whole 
camp operation is a complete health 
history of the child, including past ill¬ 
nesses, operations, allergies (to drugs, 
medications, foods, stings or insect bites, 
etc.), emotional problems or difficulties 
in adjustments. A history of the child’s 


immunization should be included. After 
being assigned their campers during 
pre-camp, counsellors should next make 
it their responsibility to learn from the 
medical stafT what, if any, health prob¬ 
lems the campers may have, and find 
out how they may help in such cases. 

From the outset, counsellors must 
realize that they do not give or take 
medications of any kind. Medical staff 
alone has the responsibility for dispens¬ 
ing all medicines and of performing all 
treatments. Pills, medicines or oint¬ 
ments which are sent in the campers’ 
trunks become the charge of the med¬ 
ical staff immediately. The reason for 
this is that a child, interested and busy, 
can easily forget to take his medicine, 
and the result might be very serious. 
In similar vein, a young inquisitive 
child could help himself to pills found 
in another camper’s trunk, with dis¬ 
astrous results. Even the common 
aspirin can be fatal in large enough 
doses. Therefore, all medicines are kept 
under lock and key in the Infirmary; 
and counsellors instructed that they are 
not permitted to help themselves to 
the contents at any time. 

From this it is obvious that no 
camper or counsellor should diagnose 
or treat himself or anyone else. For 
example, a headache is a symptom, or

ANY ZANIES TODAY? 

(Definition of Zany — one who, or 
that which, without whom directing a 
camp would be simply insupportable.) 


by Joyce Bertram, 
Camp Ouareau, Quebec . 


The young camper stood there with 
a beatific grin on her face. Her friends, 
panting and hot, steamed up the hill 
from the archery range in her wake. 
“Hey look, kids,” she shrieked, “root 
beer!” With cries of delight they crowd¬ 
ed about the water cooler, cups at the 
ready. The dark fizzy liquid bubbled 
out. There was a moment’s respect¬ 
ful silence at the thought of the muni¬ 
ficence of a camp which would provide 
its hot thirsty campers with such am¬ 
brosia. 

Suddenly shrieks of disgust and hor¬ 
ror rang out, mingled with unmistake- 
able sounds of spitting. One, quicker 
to recover than her friends, grabbed 
the lid off the cooler and looked in. 
“That’s not root beer,” she exclaimed, 
“that’s Halo shampoo!” 

Our first camper, laughing immod¬ 
erately was streaking off to the com¬ 
parative safety of the tree-house where 
only one person at a time could climb 
the ladder. 


At another camp, that same night, 
a youngster awoke with a cough and 
rose to fumble about for a box of cough 
drops. Finding them with some diffi¬ 
culty, she seized a hunting knife with 


which to pry open the lid. Returning 
from a safari to the drinking fountain 
and sucking her forbidden cough drops 
(some campers eat them like candy 
you know), she fumbled sleepily for 
the bedclothes and plunged in with¬ 
out a thought. The night air was 
rent with shrieks as of the end of the 
world. The hunting knife, lying for¬ 
gotten in the middle of the bed, had 
done its bloody work, on the only soft 
fleshy part of a twelve year old! It 
was some time before she could sit 
comfortably on the eight stitches! 


Rest Hour, ordinarily as quiet as a 
Mexican siesta was suddenly electric 
with the sound of laughter from the 
direction of the drinking fountain. Five 
or six juniors, simply convulsed, were 
grovelling about on the grass while an¬ 
other hopped about the fountain yelling 
“Here, you hold him, I’ll wash.” The 
counsellor on duty was not long in 
arriving at the scene. A toad, looking 
distinctly disgruntled was being held, 
albeit gingerly, under the stream of 
water, while several of the others tried 
vainly, with borrowed washcloths and 
soap to “wash off the mud, so he’ll 
come green again.”

Canadian Camping 


THE 

VICE-PRESIDENT’S 

PAGE 


In this province of small population, 
widely scattered and diverse communi¬ 
ties, abundant and readily accessible 
outdoor recreational areas, there is 
little awareness of camping as a re¬ 
source in the education of young people. 
The public image of camping is not 
distinct, and ranges from complete lack 
of knowledge to hazy concepts of organ¬ 
ized sports days, baseball games and 
hikes or lazy canoe trips through wilder¬ 
ness lakes. By those who do view 
camping with a broader perspective, 
attendance is still considered a luxury, 
one which is readily sacrificed when 
economic conditions fluctuate. Regular 
campers usually are second generation 
products of a small number of long 
established local camps, or they hail 
from eastern climes where camping has 
been more firmly established. 

While one hundred camps are licen¬ 
sed each year by the Provincial Govern¬ 
ment, only forty-two of these are 
listed in the most recent Camp Direc¬ 
tory, and are considered to be firmly 
established. Of these forty-two, six may 
be classed as privately owned, twenty- 
two are related to religious educational 
institutions, principally Protestant 
Churches, and the balance are associ¬ 
ated with either national youth work 
organizations or local institutions. The 
majority of non-private camps are sub¬ 
sidized. A fee of five, ten, twenty and 
twenty-five dollars per week is the usual 
fee. 


THE ASSOCIATION IN BRITISH 
COLUMBIA 

by Lome Bowering, 

Vice President, C.C.A. British Columbia, 
Director, Y.M.C.A. Camp Elphinstone 


A revival of interest in the B.C. 
Camping Association is an indication 
that significant growth is to be expected 
during the next few years. Concern is 
being expressed and the attention of 
camping people is being focused on 
three major areas: leadership, stan¬ 
dards, and the development of an 
accurate public image. 

Study is being directed to find 
methods which will lead to improved 
personnel. Effort at relating public 
educational institutions to the resident 
camp field have been made, and three 
programmes sponsored by the Extension 
Department of the University of British 
Columbia have been well attended. 

The availability of leadership is a 
problem. The young enthusiastic stu¬ 
dent of humanities is not always pre¬ 
pared to sacrifice his summer earning 
period for an indistinct and sometimes 
juvenile summer experience. High 
School students constitute the bulk of 
our leadership, and until methods of 
operation have been perfected to enable 
the recruitment of University students, 
the high school boy or girl will con¬ 
tinue to be very important. 

The implementation of minimum 
standards to provide some form of self¬ 
regulation is expected before the next 
summer season. These standards may

ON LEADING WORSHIP 

Now-a-days everybody must be 
trained, with certificates and badges to 
prove that they are capable of being 
counsellors or instructors or secretaries 
or cooks. But what about leadership in 
worship? 

O, anybody can do that! Choose a 
prayer: there are lots of books. Read 
a pretty poem. Tell a story with a 
moral. And we dare call that worship! 

Ask any minister, priest or deaconess 
and he will tell you that it requires 
years of devotion, discipline and study 
to prepare and lead in worship. Even 
with all this, no service is prepared in 
a hurry: it costs thought, time and 
worship on the leader’s part. 

This does not mean that a layman 
cannot lead in worship. Very often a 
sensitive counsellor who knows boys 
and girls, their feelings, needs and 
language, can lead in meaningful wor¬ 
ship in a way which is quite impossible 
for a large number of professionally 
trained perons who are accustomed to 
dealing with adults in a congregation. 
But that counsellor must be one who 
worships himself, to whom God is a 
reality, approachable, and concerned 
about human beings. Also there must 
be planning ahead. As a general rule 
there should be a sequence for in all 
worship there is learning too, although 
occasionally the theme of the service 
needs to be changed to suit some camp 
experience. 



by Margaret Govan 
Camp Ottawaw 


Does this rule out the practice of 
having campers take part or assist in 
the service of worship? Many camps 
consider that this is one of the places 
where the camper makes a real con¬ 
tribution. This is only true if the 
camper works beforehand with a person 
who is trained and experienced, and 
who will help him see the purposes 
and possibilities in and importance of 
such a service. Also someone who will 
explain and plan with him in his choice 
of materials. Again it takes a certain 
kind of camper, one who can lose him¬ 
self to the extent that he becomes the 
voice of the group at worship. 

If the director, or one of the section 
heads or some member of the staff, is 
incapable of leading in worship — we 
all must face and accept our limitations 
—the camp should employ just such a 
person. Of course he will have other 
responsibilities. (It would be very sad 
if campers were to think that religion 
is separated from other life experi¬ 
ences.) The person must be selected 
as you would select other staff, possess¬ 
ing the same attributes of leadership 
that you would expect of other per¬ 
sonnel. “But, where do you find such 
a person?” I can hear directors ex¬ 
postulating. What about church camp 
staff? And in order to be ethical, let’s 
trade. Most of them would be more 
than grateful for waterfront men!

HOW TO PLAN DEVOTIONS 
(adapted from the “Hi-Y Devotions Book¬ 
let” National Council of Y.M.C.A.’s of 
Canada, Toronto, 1960) 

If our worship is to be suitable to 
the occasion at hand, and if it is to be 
effective in bolstering our attempts to 
achieve our purposes; then considerable 
care should be taken in their prepara¬ 
tion and conduct To do this we must 
examine the factors which are involved 
in the planning of a worship period. 

Objective 

Prior to any planning, you must 
determine the specific objectives which 
the period is to reach. To do this you 
will have to take into consideration: 

—the relation of the worship to the 
total programme for the occasion. 
Is it supposed to set the tone for, 
or act as a climax to conclude the 
activities? 

—the direction of the worship. Is 
it to be upward-directed (i.e. 


designed to bring members closer 
to their Creator) or downward- 
directed (i.e. designed to instruct 
members according to God’s direc¬ 
tives for living) ? All worship 
periods will contain some of both 
of these elements but one or the 
other will tend to be dominant. 

Theme 

When the objectives have been 
determined, then it is essential to set 
the theme for the worship programme. 
The choice of theme will be influenced 
by the objectives of the occasion. 
Stories, scriptures, prayers and other 
items comprising the worship should be 
chosen according to the theme. 

Themes might be specific, such as 
religious holidays (i.e. Easter, Christ¬ 
mas) or general, such as moral precepts 
(i.e. honesty, sportsmanship).

BABY STINKERS! 

by Catherine VanWagner, 

Camp Nominingue, Qtie. 


It is fun to experiment with keeping 
animals at camp but only if it is fully 
understood that it is just for a matter 
of a few days or weeks. There should 
never be any question of taking them 
back to the city. 

The first year we had two baby 
skunks was fun, but by no means ex¬ 
citing just at first. They spent the day 
curled up together in a wooden box 
and then, like precocious children, they 
would wake up and play just as the 
youngest children were going to bed. 
On cold days they scratched a cover of 
dead grass over themselves and on hot 
days they went underground. In either 
case they were invisible and a dead loss 
as far as the campers were concerned. 

Some of the boys even doubted that 
we indeed had skunks at all, so that we 
were driven to waking them up about 
11:00 a.m. for a mid-morning snack. 
The boys, full of questions, crowded 
about to help and to gaze with admira¬ 
tion. Miss Muffet and Brother Tuflfy 
had been operated on very early in 
their career, but the favourite question 
was “When these two have babies will 
they be able to spray?” (History does 
not as yet record.) Muffet and Tuffy 
themselves did not seem to realize that 
they were not as other skunks, and 
many a dog on visitors’ day would beat 
a hasty retreat when faced with two 
wood pussies, with stamping feet and 
arching tail. 

After “elevenses” our tiny friends 
would go back to bed for another 


snooze. Sometimes we put a box over 
them for protection from rain or sun, 
but pushing this away soon became 
a favourite game. 

We decided to let them go free, after 
much heart-searching on the part of all 
of us. Although their natural defence had 
been taken away, we reasoned that 
half-grown skunks would not likely fall 
prey to owls or foxes, as tiny ones 
would. We also told ourselves that very 
few farmers’ dogs ever came near the 
camp. We remembered also that the 
sight of a skunk standing its ground 
was usually enough to discourage most 
natural enemies. 

“Freedom Day” arrived and we 
opened the pen. They ambled out, 
sniffing and scratching for insects and 
grasshoppers, and then wandered off 
into the woods. Tuffy lingered near 
the cabin for a few days, accepting 
tidbits and allowing me to scratch her 
neck, a thing most skunks love. But 
Miss Muffet never forgot that she was 
wild. Her experience in the pen had 
made her suspicious of people and she 
did not like being touched or picked 
up. She recognized us one night some 
months later and came close with a 
“relaxed tail” but soon went on her 
way foraging. They seemed to have 
adapted to the wild life without 
difficulty. 

We noticed small skunk tracks on the 
beach and roads during the Fall, and as 
late as November there were marks at 


106 


Canadian Camping 



the entrance to an old woodchuck hole. 
Perhaps this means that Muffet and 
Tuffy have a winter bedroom here. 
Springtime will tell the story. 

Are we going to have baby skunks 
at camp next summer? That depends 
on a lot of things. One, actually, would 
be a great deal easier, particularly if it 
had been handled and bottle-fed for a 
while. Last summer the babies were 
already weaned, had each other for 
company, and therefore were more 
independent. 

But whether we have skunks or not 
the boys who shared in the upbringing 
of Muffet and Tuffy will not soon 
forget. Perhaps Tuffy, himself, will not 
forget and will return to renew an old 
friendship. —•

professional help and it is unwise for a 
counsellor to attempt to be an amateur 
psychologist. Each individual is unique 
in his expression of his needs, and his 
behaviour is the best means he knows, 
under the circumstances, to satisfy these 
needs, despite the fact that this be¬ 
haviour may not be socially acceptable 
and gets him into difficulties. The 
causes are deeply hidden, and great 
sensitivity and understanding are re¬ 
quired in these instances. When the 
counsellor’s attention is drawn to camper 
problems, he must be ready to share 
them with the camp director or some 
other qualified, more experienced mem¬ 
ber of the staff, so as to understand 
what is involved, and to discover the 
best manner in which they can be 
handled. Something to remember is 
that the same misbehaviour does not 
always have the same cause. 

The needs of the individual camper 
can be understood only by a fairly 
complete picture of the child’s back¬ 
ground, parental relations, status in 
family environment, his potentialities, 
and in the particular group in which he

from page 105 
Duration 

It is a mark of consideration to plan 
your worship to fit the time schedule 
of the period of the day. The length 
of the programme will be determined 
by the objectives and the content of 
the programme itself. As a rule, interest 
and effectiveness are lessened by lengthy 
worship period. 

Feature 

Most programmes of any length will 
have one item in their contents which 
will be the feature item (e.g. speaker, 
story, music, ceremony). Once that 
item has been selected, the remaining 
items should be chosen and so placed 
on the programme as to highlight the 
feature as the climax. As a rule, the 
latter effect is best achieved by placing 
the feature item toward the end of the 
programme. 

Atmosphere 

Arrangements of seating and decora¬ 
tion (e.g. worship centre); and special 
effects in music and lighting will add 
to the effectiveness of the programme. 
A moment or two of meditation at the 
beginning of the period will tend to 
create the “mood” for the programme 
to follow. Music .(live talent or re¬ 
corded) during this period heightens 
the atmosphere. Special lighting can 
be used to direct members’ attention to 
the symbols on the altar or worship 
centre. As with any gathering 
attention should be given to comfort¬ 
able temperatures and sufficient ventila¬ 
tion. Gamp offers natural inspirational 
settings, such as a woodland grove, lake 
or river front, places set apart and 
secluded to provide worshipful atmos¬ 
phere. 

Materials and Equipment 

Careful planning means listing the 
materials and equipment that will be 
needed and then checking to see that 
everything is in place and on hand 
when needed during the programme.

from page 107 

finds himself at camp. As much as 
possible of this information should be 
available to the counsellor, before the 
child comes into his cabin group, or his 
area of camp programme. 

The camp programme should be 
such that each child has an opportunity 
to gain competency in some aspect of 
camp life, so that he has a position of 
belonging and status in his group. Mary 
makes her contribution through the 
camp newspaper. Fay is kept busy in 
the Intermediate Show and Religious 
Services, and Allan makes progress in 
swimming. Skills are not an end in 
themselves, but in the way they con¬ 
tribute to the individual’s adjustment. 
Children’s interests differ and camp 
should respect these differences. In 
addition, camp must widen the interests 
to suit each child and help him achieve 
desirable social practices. 

To be a well-adjusted member of a 
group, one must be ready to accept 
some of the restrictions and restraints 
which are essential for group living. 
The well-balanced person accepts these 
restraints at their true value and adapts 
his behaviour intelligently and rela¬ 
tively unemotionally, even ’though he 
may find them disagreeable and self- 
limiting. In contrast, the maladjusted 
individual feels himself incompetent to 
overcome his problems by such socially 
approved methods. Consequently, in 
order to retain his self-respect and 
position in the group, he may resort 
to aggressive behaviour or evasive tac¬ 
tics. The “show-off” demands attention 
to prove his place in the group, another 
individual may resort to day dreaming. 
Why does the camper misbehave? 
There is an excellent pamphlet by 
Kenneth Doherty, “Solving Camp Be¬ 
haviour Problems ”, that you might find 
useful. Under behaviour problems are 
listed such ones as Defiance to Disci¬ 
pline, Teasing, Quarrelling, and such 
disturbing behaviour. Children who 


are deprived of love and acceptance in 
their homes may manifest their 
emotional hunger in a variety of ways, 
ways that are used by other children 
too who have other types of problems. 
One cannot diagnose the cause of a 
behaviour problem or a personality 
problem from the symptom alone. One 
must look further. At camp, even if we 
do not have a full case history, we have 
some information to alert us to possible 
causes of deviation, and we should use 
this information to arrive at some idea 
of the child’s needs and how we should 
try to help him meet them. 

We cannot expect great miracles in 
one summer — despite the fact that 
sometimes miracles do occur. We all 
have observed spectacular positive 
changes in campers in one season. 
Sometimes these changes are not notice¬ 
able at the time, yet a contact with the 
child at a later date reveals how much 
the camping experience had meant to 
him. 

The most troublesome aspect of a 
counsellor’s job is how to be assured of 
the co-operation of his campers . The 
word “discipline” describes this require¬ 
ment, but it is so frequently misused 
that too many people regard it as a 
system of punishment to keep control 
of a situation. On the contrary, to 
discipline wisely means to get co¬ 
operation through understanding, dis¬ 
cussions and reasoning. Some time ago 
my interest was aroused by an article 
on discipline and the ten rules for a 
positive approach. I would like to pass 
these rules on to you. 

Ten Rules to Make the Job Easier 

1. Be consistent. Don’t allow at one 
time what is forbidden at another. 

2. Avoid bribery and making promises 
you can’t keep. 

3. Change your decisions only for 
good reasons, not just to end 
teasing. 

4. Don’t “horse trade.” “You do this 


108 


Canadian Camping 


—I’ll do that.” If an action is 
desirable don’t bargain. 

5. Punishment should not be humil¬ 
iating. Once administered it should 
be forgotten. 

6. Don’t threaten to withdraw affec¬ 
tion. This is as cruel as it is 
dangerous. 

7. If you must punish, make the 
punishment fit the crime. Let your 
own—and the child’s temper cool; 
the offense may not be as serious 
as it first seems. 

8. Mean business when you speak. 
Threats of future punishment are 
not as effective as handling each 
situation as it comes up. 

9. Never postpone punishment. Child¬ 
ren’s memories are short, delay 
makes punishment seem unreason¬ 
able. 

10. Set behaviour goals at a level the 
child can reach. He much prefers 
to be good, and is discouraged by 
too frequent “failures”. 

Space does not permit consideration 
of these normal problems of campers 
in detail. I wish I could give you some 
set rules for handling each problem you 
may meet. Unfortunately, there are no 
such “sure-fire” methods. What we do 
need to be equipped with, however, is 
as much information as possible about 
the child. Then, let us bring with us 

1. An attitude towards children as 
growing, developing young people 
—an attitude of acceptance of 
them as individuals, each unique 
and each needing individual under¬ 
standing. 

2. A real love of working with child¬ 
ren, not just with the pretty, 
appealing little girl or the all-round 
athlete, but with the clumsy, poorly 
co-ordinated child and the slow 
child.

from page 101 

nature’s warning that something is 
wrong. It may be a forerunner of a 
more serious illness, or may be due to 
too much sun, fatigue or constipation. 
Only when the cause has been deter¬ 
mined by the medical staff should the 
symptom be treated. It is appalling to 
note how many pain-killers, tranquilizers, 
energizers and diet pills are gobbled up 
without medical advice. The trend 
towards Do-It-Yourself in matters re¬ 
lated to health should be discouraged 
most vigorously. Campers and coun¬ 
sellors should, again, be instructed not 
to treat cuts, blisters, burns or scalds, 
remove slivers or remove foreign bodies 
from the eye. A minor skin abrasion 
can flare into a nasty infection. The 
medical staff is employed to perform 
these duties, and the responsibility rests 
with them. 

Diet 

In some instances parents hope that 
during their stay at camp campers’ 
eating habits will improve. Counsellors 
can go far in encouraging them by 
setting a good example in eating full 
meals themselves. If they eat “some¬ 
thing of everything” that comes to the 
table, campers will follow suit; and this 
should not be too unpleasant, camp 
food being the good food it usually is- 
If counsellors complain and become 
choosey, campers will too. It should 
be made quite clear to them, also, that 
self-imposed diets can be as harmful 
to themselves as they are to the needs 
and development of growing children. 

On the other hand, information and 
recommendations concerning food all¬ 
ergies, metabolic conditions or the 
desirability of weight control made by 
the family doctor on the camper’s 
health form come under the supervision 
of the medical staff. Counsellors should 
be given the particulars, if any such 
conditions exist, and they should keep

a close check on the camper at meal 
time, snack time and on out-trips. 

Out of Camp 

It is the duty of medical staff to 
adequately train counsellors who are to 
be in charge of campers away from 
camp on canoe trips, hikes or cook-outs. 
Staff must know’ something of basic 
first aid, and have a knowledge of the 
steps to take in any conceivable 
emergency. 

All trips away from the camp site 
must be equipped with a First Aid Kit. 
Before the trip leaves, the counsellor 
in charge must receive instruction on 
the use of its contents. It must be in 
the hands of one counsellor on the 
trip, and easily available on top of one 
specific pack at all times. The coun¬ 
sellor returns it to the Infirmary at 
once at the end of the trip to be 
cleaned and replenished. 

Warmth and Comfort 

It is hoped that in preparing the 
child for camp, the director has made 
it quite clear that Thongs are forbidden 
for camp use at any time. Counsellors 
should understand that this type of 
inadequate footwear has been respon¬ 
sible for serious accidents, sprained and 
broken ankles and severely stubbed and 
cut toes, through many a trip and fall. 
Counsellors should be asked to supervise 
campers to see that proper shoes or 
sneakers are worn at all times. 

If the child should arrive at camp 
without a sturdy raincoat and hat, sun 
hat, rubber boots, sufficient warm cloth¬ 
ing or an inadequate supply of wool 
blankets, the counsellor should be alert 
enough to notify the director, so that 
the forgotten items can be requested 
from home by the next mail. 

It is vitally important that campers 
be warm all through the night. The 
director can ask his counsellors to see 
that campers sleep in socks and a 
sweater over pyjamas if there is any 
possibility of dampness or a drop in 


110 


Canadian Camping 



temperature. Many lists of Suggested 
Items now include a hot water bottle 
for very cold nights. 

There is much to be said in favour 
of the counsellor being aware of the 
Health Department rules and regula¬ 
tions. The following are excellent topics 
for discussion groups in pre-camp: 

The use of Halizone Tablets or 
Chlorination Kits. 

The proper storage of foods, so 
that consumption of contamin¬ 
ated sandwich fillings, creamed 
foods and other left-overs on 
out-trips can be avoided. 

Sanitary dishwashing procedures. 

Disposal of garbage. 

Reasons for frequent washing of 
hands. 

In placing a portable roll-up type 
stretcher at a central point of camp, 
say the waterfront, an emergency could 
be handled without unnecessary delay. 
Instruction should be provided and a 
quick drill routine organized. 

Staff requirements include: 

A pre-camp medical and dental 
check-up, including immuniza¬ 
tion. 

A full supply of needs for camp— 
flashlights, batteries, kleenex, 
sanitary supplies, sleeping bag, 
raincoat, blankets. 

Many of these items are borrowed 
without permission from the 
campers, a habit which should 
be discouraged since it causes 
annoyance and loss of respect on 
the part of the campers. 

Good Example 

We have said that counsellors can 
influence positively through their own 
good example, and must know that a 
“do as I say, not as I do” approach 
contributes directly to failure in dis¬ 
cipline and co-operation. It is essential 
that staff members practice good 
grooming, even in the relaxed atmos¬ 
phere of camp, by regular washing,

At a boys’ camp they were having 
a barbecue in honour of Father and 
Son Week-end. Two boys who had 
proudly displayed the cam]) to their 
father were in the crowd gathered 
about the barbecue eagerly awaiting 
dinner. A large pig was being slowly 
roasted on a spit and the smell had 
been tantalizing the hungry crowd for 
some hours. That is, all except one of 
the brothers who had been heard to 
say at fifteen-minute intervals most of 
the day, “I’m not having any of that 
old dead pig. Why can’t they give us 
something decent, like hamburgers?” 

In due time “that old dead pig” was 
ready and the younger brother, being 
more intrepid, or perhaps more raven¬ 
ous, decided to chance it. Despite his 
brother’s grumbling and protestations, 
he lined up with his plate. Gingerly 
he took a mouthful and a beatific smile 
spread across his face. Then he broke 
into a run. “Hey Mike,” he yelled, 
“You should try some. It tastes just 
like meat.” 


Some nature lovers at a camp in 
Haliburton had acquired a snapping 
turtle (don’t ask me why) and had 
made a small cage for it, part on land 
and part in the water. Campers were 
electrified one day to see their handi¬ 
crafts counsellor solemnly stalking up 
and down the shoreline in about two 
feet of water, with a dog’s lead in her 
hand. Closer inspection revealed that 
the leash was attached to the turtle 
and that it was being taken for a walk 
“to stretch its legs.” “Turtling” ins¬ 
tantly took its place in the camp pro¬ 
gramme and the line formed on the 
left for the privilege of escorting Turtle 
on its daily perambulations. 


112 


Canadian Camping 





A counsellor at one camp had a 
group of fairly lazy campers who had 
elected to go on a cook out. The 
counsellor discovered to her dismay 
that she was expected to do most of 
the work. Staunchly refusing to do so, 
she taught the kids how to gather fire¬ 
wood, how to light a fire, how to soap 
a pot, how to cook and how to clean 
up. It was tough going and lunch did 
not appear until 3:30. The following 
week when it was suggested that they 
go again, the counsellor was more pre¬ 
pared. When the campers had beached 
their canoes and had had a swim they 
said plaintively, “What do we do now?” 
Solemnly unwrapping a parcel she re¬ 
plied, “You can do what you like— 
I’m planning to eat my lunch.” Saying 
which she started in on the ham sand¬ 
wiches and doughnuts which the kit¬ 
chen had thoughtfully provided. Lunch 
that day was ready by 3:00! 


A camp in Quebec decided to plant 
500 Scotch pine, one very rainy week 
in August. Bundles of seedlings having 
been acquired, campers were assembled 
and every spade, shovel and trowel of 
every description was pressed into ser¬ 
vice. Juniors armed themselves with 
large spoons from the trip shed. A 
camper was chosen from each section to 
be in charge of giving out the tiny 
trees and to supervise the actual terrain 
where they were to be planted. Much 
actively for over an hour! The Seniors, 
bigger and stronger, naturally finished 
first. The Intermediates, although hav¬ 
ing more trees to plant, finished second. 
It was some time before anyone noticed 
that the Juniors, who had only 100 
trees between them, were taking an 
interminable time. Observers watched

from page 97 

and the camp reunion is a necessary 
means towards this end. Informal 
gatherings at inter-varsity games, at 
weddings and anniversaries, or several 
informal Sunday afternoon teas during 
the year will do much to create the 
teamwork necessary for a successful 
summer. 

Camp Hospitality 

The manner in which ex-staff mem¬ 
bers are treated if they visit during the 
summer is an important factor in staff 
relations' Present staff are quick to 
sense the difference between a genuine 
welcome and a brush-off. Regardless 
of his or her former position at camp 
an ex-staff member usually has a good 
reason for a return visit, mostly nostal¬ 
gic. A genuine welcome goes a long 
way towards convincing this year’s 
staff that the director is sincere. It 
should be clearly understood that no 
liquor is to be brought in by visitors. 
Any smoking or safety rules applying 
to staff should be observed by visiting 
ex-staff and it would seem reasonable 
that if they are visiting a friend they 
would not expect the friend to neglect 
his duties in order to visit with them. 
Camp policy with regard to counsel¬ 
lors’ time off when visitors arrive 
should be stated in pre-camp sessions. 
The director must also state clearly the 
rules about overnight or meal accom¬ 
modation for visiting counsellors, par¬ 
ents or friends. 

The use of the term Director of 
Programme is becoming obsolete in 
many camps, and in its place is a much 
more functional title, Programme Co¬ 
ordinator. Good staff relations often 
depend on the satisfactions derived by 
the staff from their tasks. The more 
creative the job, the more involved the 
person, the more he regards the enter¬ 
prise with respect. Programme Direc¬ 
tors tend to get all the credit without 
always deserving it. Camp activities 
provide many opportunities for emer¬ 


gent leadership. Camp fires, Circuses, 
Final Banquet, Regattas — all afford 
opportunities for many staff members 
to head up some programme, chair 
the planning committee, make an¬ 
nouncements, etc. The Programme 
Co-ordinator functions as a helper, ar¬ 
ranges for equipment, meeting places 
and so on. The spotlight of recogni¬ 
tion focuses on many individuals. Fu¬ 
ture leaders emerge and that Good 
Feeling dominates the oamp. 

Contracts 

A contract setting out conditions of 
work, amount of pay and dates of ser¬ 
vice is an essential camp document. 
Vague promises and “understandings” 
have a way of losing any original 
meaning as the summer develops. 
There should be no juggling with the 
terms of a contract. If part of the 
employee’s pay includes free camping 
for his or her children, such should be 
stated. Any attempt to avoid income 
tax by “special arrangements” places 
the camp and the staff at a disadvan¬ 
tage. Conscientious effort and positive 
criticism find it difficult to flourish in 
an atmosphere of dishonesty. Minor 
altercations are always possible and 
they are much more difficult to resolve 
if it is possible for either party to resort 
to subtle blackmail. 

Staff Behaviour 

How much freedom of action and 
behaviour can be left to the discretion 
of the staff? Some camps are firm and 
uncompromising with respect to rules 
about smoking, drinking, hours of re¬ 
tirement and so on. Providing every¬ 
one understands and accepts these 
conditions, misunderstanding can be 
avoided. If the directors and senior 
staff fail to observe such rules them¬ 
selves or if a few of the staff are per¬ 
mitted to get away with infractions, 
morale suffers. Staff conduct should 
be related to the aims and objectives 
of the camp. There should be no com¬ 
promise about liquor and with our 


114 


Canadian Camping 



enlightened knowledge about the 
harmful effects of cigarette smoking, it 
is just possible that a staff may want 
to set up conditions that would help 
addicts break the habit. Smoking 
should be confined to areas away from 
campers and where there is a mini¬ 
mum fire hazard. What to do about 
staff smoking on canoe trips is a real 
problem. Sometimes a straight-for¬ 
ward request is much more effective 
without threat of consequences or 
punishment. 

Any compromise with respect to 
liquor is fraught with danger. It is no 
real hardship for anyone engaged in 
camping to refrain from alcohol in the 
camp setting. To forbid its use when 
staff are away from camp on a day off, 
however, conflicts with our concept of 
personal freedom. The policy can and 
should be stated to prevent anyone 
returning to the camp under the in¬ 
fluence of liquor since their co-opera¬ 
tion might be required in an emerg¬ 
ency. In addition to a statement of 
such policy on the contract it is a good 
practice to emphasize this matter in 
the pre-camp training session and oc¬ 
casionally throughout the summer in 
staff meetings. Even at the risk of 
losing the services of an effective staff 
member it pays in the long run to en¬ 
force this policy with dismissal if proof 
is evident that it is not being observed. 

Fatigue 

The physical and emotional de¬ 
mands on a staff involved in supervis¬ 
ing the activities of children require 
adequate rest and recreation. This 
factor is one of the most difficult mat¬ 
ters to convey to young staff members. 
Few camps succeed in solving the pro¬ 
blem, either with authoritarian rules 
or laissez faire appeals to reason. Fa¬ 
tigue will set in and morale does lower. 
A frank realization of this will at least 
prepare the director to deal with it as 
it occurs during the summer, and paves 
the way for a concerted effort for im¬ 


mediate solution. The alert director 
anticipates fatigue and makes certain 
the topic appears on the agenda of 
meetings throughout the summer. In¬ 
dividual counselling of the more obvi¬ 
ous offenders is often successful and 
sometimes an enforced day of rest (to 
be counted as a day off) seems to be 
justified. Rules about bed-time don’t 
seem to work since some require less 
sleep than others. Then, too, there 
are always those individuals who seem 
better able to pace themselves than 
others. The real test is always the 
ability of the staff member to do his 
job the following day or days. 

The practice now is for the working 
schedule of each staff member to pro¬ 
vide for at least one-half to one day a 
week free from responsibility and at 
least two hours every day free from 
camp duties. This should hold true 
for the director too. Ask the staff! 

Gamps are finding that it is neces¬ 
sary to have a policy regarding staff 
automobiles. Young staff members 
away from parental guidance some¬ 
times require regulations that will per¬ 
mit them to operate within safe limits. 
Here again the staff is capable of 
drawing up realistic rules once the rea¬ 
son is clear. The legal driving age of 
sixteen is considered too low by many 
camps. Where the minimum counsel¬ 
lor age is eighteen, many organizations 
find that it pays to include a statement 
in the contract to the effect that any¬ 
one under the minimum counsellor age 
should not plan on driving his or her 
car during the summer. 

Snacks 

One of the indications of advancing 
years for the camp director is when he 
becomes appalled at the amount of 
food a staff will consume at an evening 
function. Young people, engaged in 
healthy outdoor activity develop insa¬ 
tiable appetites. The availability of 
night food is an important factor in

staff relations. Denied access to even¬ 
ing snacks, staffs have been known to 
pilfer, hoard or leave camp for the 
nearest store. Organized with a view 
to avoiding waste and not requiring 
extra working time on the part of the 
kitchen staff, the fare should be plain 
and plentiful. Every night of the week 
is not too often for this to be available. 

Staff Supervision 

Supervisory conferences have been 
going on -at camp for many years but 
usually on a hit and miss basis and 
without clear cut objectives. There 
are at least five good reasons for sched¬ 
uling such conferences during the sum¬ 
mer with all staff members. In a very 
large camp the chore will have to be 
shared -and it should be carried out at 
least twice and more often where the 
need is obvious. Such supervisory con¬ 
ferences will: 

1. Strengthen the co-operative relation¬ 
ship between staff member and 
camp director. 

2. Provide specific help to the counsel¬ 
lor or instructor. 

3. Sharpen up the central aims and 
objectives of the camp. 

4. Provide a definite time and setting 
for looking at the educational pro¬ 
cess. 

5. Provide an opportunity for commen¬ 
dation. (A time for reprimand is 
usually always found—not so for 
commendation.) 

Before the supervisor can engage the 
cabin leader or activity instructor in a 
meaningful discussion of his work, he 
should plan to make a “supervisory 
observation”. A good beginning is the 
staff application file and then camper 
records. Try to see a wide range of 
activity. Note such factors as the phy¬ 
sical setting. What the group has done 
to enhance or individualize their oabin 
or environs is often significant. Try 
to observe inter-personal relationships 


116 


Canadian Camping 



—the way group members get along 
or relate one to the other and what the 
counsellor does about it. Note his tech¬ 
niques of leadership—how he uses the 
strengths of group members and pro¬ 
vides support when needed. Observe 
the content of the programme, and 
when you are satisfied you have really 
seen this person at work, talk with him 
about his feelings and your observa¬ 
tions. 

When a supervisor observes the work 
of a counsellor or other staff member 
according to a plan, the following val¬ 
ues accrue: 

1. He is provided with first hand, ob¬ 
jective information about the group 
and the counsellor’s relation to its 
members. 

2. He is able to see the methods em¬ 
ployed by the counsellor in action. 

3. The experience helps to establish a 
positive relationship between the 
supervisor and the counsellor. 

4. The supervisor sees conditions as 
they really are—not as reported. 

5. Because of the experience and ability 
of the supervisor, individual needs 
of group members can be identified. 

6. The experiences gained in these 
supervisory periods provide concrete 
material for conferences with the 
counsellor. 

7. The “stuff” of observations assists in 
evaluating the effectiveness of the 
camp. 

8. Data for determining objectives and 
content of camp programme for staff 
meetings comes from such observa¬ 
tions. Great care must be taken to 
•avoid embarrassment to staff by pin¬ 
pointing weaknesses in such sessions. 

The process of evaluating staff mem¬ 
bers may be expected to carry over 
into an evaluation of the camp and its 
programme. When this occurs there is 
reason for the camp director to believe 
he is succeeding in his aim to develop 
good teamwork.

Mention should be made of some old 
chestnuts that result in good team¬ 
work. Many camps now have mimeo¬ 
graphed outlines of the various jobs, 
which are sent to staff in the late 
spring. An organization chart which 
answers the question, “Where do I fit 
in?” is a useful device. Replacing the 
old camp leaders’ training courses, 
which are difficult to arrange because 
of the increased demands on the time 
of students, is the pre-camp training 
session on the actual campsite. Here 
the group tackles problems that apply 
to their own camp. The discussions are 
meaningful because everyone knows 
that in a few days’ time the campers 
will arrive and a job has to be done. 
A small planning group, meeting early 
in the spring, might organize the pre¬ 
camp training period. 

Staff Meetings 

Staff meetings have a direct bearing 
on staff relations. Meetings are pri¬ 
marily for the communication of ideas 
and information, and in a camp all the 
information and all the ideas are not 
the exclusive property of one man. 
There are two very real problems con¬ 
nected with staff meetings. The first is 
when to hold them and the second is 
how to make them purposeful and 
meaningful. There is no easy solution 
to either of these problems. While it 
is desirable to have all the staff present 
it is inconceivable that campers should 
be left without supervision. Days off, 
and canoe trips also prevent a full 
turn out. In very large camps the 
staff meet as sections with only the 
leaders gathering to discuss major 
camp policy. The other problem con¬ 
cerns the atmosphere of the meeting, 
and this is dependent upon many fac¬ 
tors. The most important ingredient, 
however, is the attitude of the camp 
director. The manner in which he 
responds to suggestions, his philosophy, 
his knowledge of group work, his sin¬ 
cerity of purpose, all determine the 


118 


Canadian Camping 




extent to which the staff will risk them¬ 
selves in the meeting. If an inexperi¬ 
enced staff person is even slightly ridi¬ 
culed because his idea is poorly formu¬ 
lated or expressed, if the director ex¬ 
presses impatience, if he vetoes too 
many group suggestions: his behaviour 
will prevent the communication of 
ideas. If the director will bear in mind 
that his relationship with the staff is 
likely to be the same as the relationship 
between individual staff members and 
the campers, perhaps he will practice 
the control, humility and regard for 
others that mark the true leader. 

It is generally accepted that no one 
ever really owns a cat. The same is 
true of a camp. Perhaps this realiza¬ 
tion needs to be fully understood by 
the camp director if he hopes to 
achieve good teamwork and staff rela¬ 
tions. While it is true that the director 
puts his stamp on the camp, the total 
effect is such a composite that it has 
to be bigger than one person. Gamp 
is not a property, a group of buildings. 
It is an experience, a different experi¬ 
ence for every camper and every staff 
member. As long as our camp direc¬ 
tors understand they are proprietors 
of a trust rather than owners of camps, 
Canadian parents will continue to en¬ 
trust their children to their care. 


AN INTRODUCTION TO 
NATURE STUDY 

FOR SUMMER CAMPS 
P . Af. Taschereau 

This twenty-page publication touches 
lightly on a wide range of nature topics 
with a view to providing camp leaders 
with a loose-leaf sized working manual 
to camp nature study, and of “Whetting 
their appetites” to follow further into 
more detailed and specialized texts. It 
is effectively illustrated with drawings 
by R. S. Robertson and photographs by 
the author. You will glean ideas from 
his suggestions on Fitting Nature Study 
into the Camp Programme, The Nature 
Hike and Nature Trails, Nature Activi¬ 
ties and Crafts, The Camp Museum, 
Collections and Collecting. Nova Scotia 
Museum of Science, Spring Garden 
Road, Halifax, N.S. 75c to individuals; 
50c to educational institutions or in¬ 
dividuals purchasing more than 10 
copies. —•

from page 111 

brushing of teeth, wearing of clean 
clothing, and a simple, neat hair-do, 
keeping their quarters reasonably tidy, 
and conforming themselves to the basic 
rules of health and safety. This includes 
the wearing of sun hats, the wearing of 
shoes, dressing according to the weather, 
keeping reasonable hours, not taking 
chances or undertaking foolhardy stunts 
on water or land. Otherwise counsellors 
cannot expect much respect from their 
campers, nor can they control their 
groups. Any child will naturally react 
with a Why-Should-I-The-Counsellor- 
Doesn’t attitude. 

It must be remember, too, that all 
these rules apply to every person who 
is in camp, whether maintenance staff, 
camp members or visiting relatives and 
friends; and this includes the Director . 
Leadership and example begin at the 
top, and come down the line through 
staff to campers. 

The camping experience can be a 
happy and rewarding adventure only 
if safety and health come first. —*

Canadian Camping Association 
Annual Meeting 

The Canadian Camping Association 
held its annual meeting at the Banff 
School of Fine Arts on February 7 th, 
1964. All the provincial bodies were 
represented. Dr. W. D. Smith, the 
President, was in the chair. 

The reports from the provinces were 
interesting and varied, although all 
were concerned about camp standards; 
and almost all about seminars and 
conferences. Some provincial associa¬ 
tions are very active in the number of 
meetings that they hold, for the total 
membership, throughout the year. 

The Ontario Camping Association 
sponsored the visits of Jamaican older 
boys and girls who are expected to 
give camp leadership in their own 
country; this had proved most satis¬ 
factory. 

Dr. Smith reported on the Centenary 
Journey, and paid the Camping Mag¬ 
azine a compliment. One of the matters 
of concern is the present constitution 
of C.C.A. which has not proved 
workable. 

The annual meeting was held in 
connection with a seminary on leader¬ 
ship. Dr. Hedley Dimock Jr. gave a 
course of five lectures which were most 
helpful. About eighty persons were 
present. _* 


HOME-STUDY COURSE IN 
CAMPING PLANNED 

Plans for development of a home- 
study course in camp direction have 
been announced by Howard P. Gallo¬ 
way, president of Galloway Publishing 
Co., and editor and publisher of Camp¬ 
ing Magazine. This new service will 
be offered by the newly-formed Gallo¬ 
way Career Advancement School. 

A well-qualified Guiding Faculty has 
been appointed to assist in development 
of material for the course, and they are 
currently planning basic context of 
lessons and their arrangement into 
logical learning order. Following this, 
the School’s Curriculum Committee will 
meet for development of the course 
syllabus and selection of study materials. 
After review by the Guiding Faculty, 
the course will be presented to the New 
Jersey State Department of Education 
for approval and licensing of the 
School. The course will then be made 
available to anyone wishing to add to 
his knowledge and ability in camp 
operation. 

For further information write to 
Galloway Career Advancement School, 
1114 South Ave., Plainfield, N.J. 

—•
