BOOKS 

For Your 
CAMP LIBRARY 

Reviewed 

by Eanswythe Flynn 


MUSKOKA AND HALIBURTON 

Florence B. Murray 

The hopes and heartbreaks, the en¬ 
thusiasms and fears connected with the 
discovery and early development of 
these two areas of Ontario have been 
settled into one volume, though not in 
the conventional style of a romantic 
novel. Miss Murray, an Associate 
Professor at the Library School, Uni¬ 
versity of Toronto, has spent many years 
gathering the documents, diaries and 
personal stories that go into the making 
of such an accurate and absorbing 
history. That it is a complete book of 
reference on the subject, there is no 
doubt. From the day that Etienne 
Brule set foot in the area in 1610, as 
the first European to do so, to the late 
1800’s, she highlights the districts of 
Severn, Bala and Parry Sound, Minden, 
Haliburton and Dorset, Huntsville, 
Bracebridge and Gravenhurst, as far 
east as Bancroft, Gooderham, Irondale 
and Kinmount, as well as outlining the 
military aspect of the Monck Road. A 
Baedecker for tourists, an encylopaedia 
for businessmen, a history and reference 
book for camp directors and family 
camping groups. Miss Murray’s collec¬ 
tion of documents parallels Edith G. 
Firth’s THE TOWN OF YORK, as an 
important part of the reference shelf 
in home, office or camp. University of 
Toronto Press. $5.00. 


We salute Canadian Library Week this April 
with the following review of two story books 
to read to campers . 


NUNNY BAG 2 

For Six-to-Nine-Year-Olds 

RUBABOO 2 

for Ten-to-TwelveYear-Olds 

Two perfectly good Canadian names, 
the titles themselves hold our interest. 
For the enlightenment of all of us: 
Rubaboo is a stew made from pemmi- 
can, flour, water, potatoes, wild onions, 
savoury herbs and vegetables, which 
nourished our Canadian Indians and 
sustained Canadian explorers, particu¬ 
larly in the West. A Nunny Bag is a 
draw-string bag which could hold any¬ 
thing. Our mother had one of intricate 
pattern, crocheted in string of a lush 
shade of mellowed forest green. An 
artist would use burlap, perhaps; a 
camper, one of canvas; a nunny bag 
for shoes could be made of any fabric 
from velvet to calico. 

Both books, second in the publisher’s 
“Writing for Young Canada ” series, 
hold chapter after chapter of delightful 
Canadian stories, fresh, original, and 
reminiscent of Hans Andersen or 
Grimm. The authors hail from every 
province in the Dominion, each with 
his or her own way of bringing fantasy 
and poesy, with an element of excite¬ 
ment, to the mind of the child. In 
reading them to children, you will find 
the Indian legends, the myths, imagin¬ 
ings and adventures most appealing; a 
sound influence in shaping their taste 
towards a high standard in language 
and artistic integrity. W. J. Gage, 
Limited. 


122 


Canadian Camping 




LEADING TEEN-AGE GROUPS 

Dorothy M. Roberts 

So often Camp Counsellors and 
Teachers have remarked on the difficul¬ 
ties in communicating with teen agers. 
For those who have a talent for teach¬ 
ing this group, there is little or no 
problem. For those who haven’t that 
ability, the struggle is ever-present. In 
this new book, Dorothy Roberts has 
called on her experience over many 
years, and in varied fields, of work in 
youth leadership with the YMCA of 
New York State, and in city, church 
and suburban groups. She has a way 
of easing the load for leaders who must 
organize young people into groups, in 
looking at the Teenager as a whole self 
who is, in the vast majority, more than 
eager to grow into a complete, useful 
and responsible adult. The author is 
wise in giving her advice, experienced 
in showing how to lead this age group, 
and understanding in helping those 
who deal with our boys and girls of 
today. G. R. Welch & Co., Toronto. 
$4.25. 


DROWNPROOFING! 

A New Technique for Water Safety 
Fred R. Lanoue 

This book is a well prepared, easily 
understood piece of resource on drown¬ 
proofing. It contains a good course 
method of teaching drownproofing, and 
a good rundown on various technical 
aspects of swimming. 

Much has been said on the question 
of drownproofing, but I do feel that in 
this book we find most of the answers. 
The various swimming organizations in 
Canada are using the book. This, I 
am sure, is due in part to the fine use 
of illustrations. To those who are look¬ 
ing for a clear and concise interpreta¬ 
tion of the new travelling stroke, I say 
take a look at this book. It is certainly 
a good investment for any camp which 
contemplates using drownproofing in its 
camp programme. Prentice-Hall, 1963, 
$4.75. 

—Norm McKee, A.S.T.A. 

Y.M.C.A. Aquatic Commissioner 
for Ontario 

Director, Camp Ki-Wa-Y.

BRADFORD WOODS 
MARTINSVILLE — INDIANA 


front page 98 

to make positive use of them through 
publications and proper marking of the 
routes themselves. 

The Association feels there are other 
reasons for advocating such a Centenary 
Project. It would emphasize the fact 
that Canadian history extends back 
several centuries into history and, if 
authentic means of transportation are 
used, would commemorate the canoe, 
the freight canoe, the schooner, the 
pack train and perhaps the bateau. 

Such a Centenary Project would also 
illustrate, to Canadians and others, the 
fascination of our geology: the wonder¬ 
land of lakes and rivers and the extent 
of so many of our natural resources. 
It would, of course, provide a real 
challenge to many citizens in this age 
of luxury, soft living, lack of care or 
interest in physical fitness, and tensions. 
It would give Canadians the oppor¬ 
tunity to re-think their position in our 
modern world and, perhaps, re-evaluate 
the contributions Canada can make in 
a period characterized by an exploding 
population, food shortages, rising totali¬ 
tarianism, amid a general air of sus¬ 
picion, selfishness and violence. 

Finally, such a project could well 
develop into a continuing resource for 
Canadians to develop self-reliance, fit¬ 
ness, proper insight into history and 
geography and the natural environment 
of Canada. It would promote under¬ 
standing of the fact that Canada is a 
nation built of many parts, each one 
of which has made its own significant 
contribution to our common weal — 
beginning with the Indian and Eskimo 
and leading to the New Canadian of 
to-day and tomorrow. 

What route would the proposed 
Centenary Project follow? The Atlantic 
Provinces, not being part of the historic 
“water highways” to the west, would 
have to develop schooner runs or canoe 


124 


Canadian Camping 













































trips over waters of historic importance 
but which may not necessarily have 
been associated with the fur trade. 

From the St. Lawrence the route 
would be the historic one used by 
Indians, voyageurs and traders alike: 
beginning at Lachine, ascending the 
Ottawa and Mattawa rivers, crossing 
Lake Nipissing, descending the French 
River, traversing the northern waters 
of Lakes Huron and Superior. From 
the site of “Grand Portage” at the head 
of Lake Superior where the Nor* Westers 
of the late eighteenth century staged 
their annual celebrations and completed 
their trade transactions — they also 
changed from their big Montreal canoes 
(canots de maitre to smaller inland 
canoes (canots du nord)—from this 
site the route generally follows the 
International Boundary to Lake of the 
Woods. The rivers of the prairies, of 
the British Columbia coast and the 
Rockies and the MacKenzie in the 
north west, are all legitimate parts of 
the all-embracing “voyageurs highway”. 
An excellent reference work is Mr. Eric 
Morse’s “The Routes of the Voyageurs”, 
originally published in the Canadian 
Geographic Magazine. 

How is such a Centenary Project to 
be carried out? There are several 
essential steps. 

First, setting up provincial com¬ 
mittees sponsored by the provincial 
Camping Associations. Members will 
also be drawn as well from organiza¬ 
tions active in outdoors work, conser¬ 
vation, local history, etc. These 
committees will be responsible for the 
selection of the final routes (which must 
meet properly at provincial borders) 
and perhaps alternatives that have par¬ 
ticular historical significance. After this 
the task of setting up route markers 
would have to be arranged and carried 
out. 


Obviously, work would have to start 
as soon as possible, in order that canoe¬ 
ing teams in each province may set out 
and actually cover the route or series of 
routes in their respective regions. At the 
same time, adequate historical research 
must be carried out (or located if al¬ 
ready available), as well as preparation 
of markers and publications explaining 
and illustrating the significance of both 
markers and routes. 

At all times, there must be proper 
co-ordination and exchange of informa¬ 
tion between committees sponsored by 
the Camping Associations and the Com¬ 
mittees in each province which have 
been established to handle Centenary 
projects within their borders. 

At all times, proper advantage must 
be taken of all publicity possibilities: 
during the research, during the inspec¬ 
tion and selection of routes, during the 
marker. Every one of these preliminary 
stages will contain items or elements of 
interest to daily and weekly newspapers, 
national consumer magazines, radio and 
television stations and perhaps net¬ 
works. The filming possibilities are 
obvious and where possible every team 
setting out to inspect or mark a route 
should be equipped to bring back both 
still and motion pictures. It may also 
be possible to interest Canada’s National 
Film Board in producing a documen¬ 
tary film on the subject, or to induce 
a national business organization to 
sponsor such a film if made by a private 
Canadian production company. 

It should be emphasized very early 
in the project that modern means of 
transportation will be frowned on or 
actually prohibited. This would apply 
to outboard engines, particularly on 
large open stretches of water (e.g. Lake 
Superior). Wherever possible other 
community “human resources” should 
be used: Chambers of Commerce or 
Boards of Trade will give enthusiastic

CAMP, in the Lake of 
Bays District, Muskoka, Ontario. 
Camp has accommodation for 
100 campers plus staff. Property 
consists of 135 acres, with / 2 to 
% mile of good shoreline. There 
are 30 buildings, including large 
dining-room and recreation hall,

from page 95 

groups, Fielder found that the “leaders” 
of effective groups had a certain social 
distance from their followers. Other 
studies focus on this point and suggest 
that members who are well accepted 
by the group, but are slightly aloof in 
that they don’t act like “one of the 
boys”, are the most likely to perform 
leadership acts. It is not that members 
will not respect a person with whom 
they are too familiar, but rather that a 
“leader” who is too close to his fol¬ 
lowers finds it hard to reach decisions 
without being influenced by his feelings. 
People most effective in inter-personal 
relations are able to differentiate among 
members of a group along a variety 
of personality dimensions. The best 
basketball captain can describe a com¬ 
prehensive set of weaknesses and 
strengths for each team player and does 
not tend to see several players as “about 
the same”. 

Acceptance or popularity in a group 
seems to be a prerequisite to the success¬ 
ful completion of leadership acts. Socio¬ 
metric methods for determining 
acceptance have been rather accurate 
in predicting degree of leadership. A 
high sociometric position contributes to 
leadership by providing individuals with 
a receptive audience, a channel for 
influence and communication, and some 
prestige or power in the eyes of others. 
Social-economic status is an important 
factor affecting acceptance in many 
groups. 

In StogdilPs (1957) extensive studies 
of leadership four factors appeared to 
effectively describe leader behaviour: 
consideration; initiation of structure; 
production emphasis; and sensitivity 
(social awareness). Showing considera¬ 
tion for other group members accounted 
for fifty percent of the leadership 
dimensions. People who identify and 
respond to the emotional needs are most 
likely to provide group leadership. 

6 


126 


Canadian Camping 



Members who are above average in 
leadership show more empathy or 
understanding of others and are also 
more accurate in ability to judge other 
members’ feelings and opinions on issues 
relevant to the group. 

Research also indicates that the per¬ 
son who does most of the talking is most 
likely to influence the group and be¬ 
come accepted as a leader providing 
he doesn’t talk so much that he an¬ 
tagonizes the other group members. It is 
likely that those who emerge as leaders 
are more vocal and dominant, and 
push the group toward its goals. They 
may assume these roles because they 
are more highly motivated to the 
group’s tasks than other members or 
they may have greater needs to control 
the group and exercise power. Cer¬ 
tainly, any member who can communi¬ 
cate more frequently or in any way 
controls communication in the group 
(such as the discussion chairman) is 
more likely to be a “leader” than one 
who does not. Bavelas (1960) has 
manipulated leadership among mem¬ 
bers of experimental groups by shifting 
the channels of communication to flow 
through various members in order to 
illustrate this principle. 

In summary, then, camps looking for 
effective leaders for their staff positions 
would do well to consider the following 
criteria: 

1. normal or above intelligence 

2. emotional and social maturity 
(social sensitivity) 

3. ability to observe and discriminate 
among people 

4. competence in personal relation¬ 
ships (shows consideration and 
initiates structure) 

5. empathy and understanding of 
others feelings and responses 

6. ability to communicate openly and 
freely.

from page 127 

Style of Leadership of the 
Camp Counsellor 

Some counsellors encourage campers 
to share the leadership functions in 
the group and assume whatever re¬ 
sponsibility is within their capacity. 
Other counsellors tend to dominate the 
group, give direction for all activities 
and accept all responsibility for what 
happens .(good and bad). The former 
is referred to as group-centered or 
democratic, while the latter is domin¬ 
ant leadership which is basically 
autocratic. 

Countless studies have measured the 
differences in effect on group behaviour 
and individual growth of group- 
centered and dominant leadership. 
These studies, carried out in children’s 
groups, classrooms, business and in¬ 
dustry and in family groups all agree 
that group-centered leadership is most 
likely to achieve the desired objectives 
in these different situations. In specific 
reference to youth camp groups, group- 
centered counsellors are most likely to 
help campers enjoy the experience; 
develop friendly, co-operative and 
socially constructive relationships; be¬ 
come more self-reliant and responsible, 
showing initiative and creativity in new 
situations; and develop more stable 
emotional characteristics (less suscep¬ 
tible to character or behaviour 
disorders). It is also clear that group- 
centered leaders develop more healthy 
groups that have a more positive in¬ 
fluence on their members than do 
dominating leaders. 

Research has also shown that super¬ 
visors (and we can assume that camp 
directors fit this conclusion) who are 
group-centered have workers who pro¬ 
duce the most, have the highest morale, 
and the lowest rate of absences and 
turnover. These supervisors, by co¬ 
operating closely with their work group 
and involving them in decisions which 


affect them, are also most able to ex¬ 
periment with more effective methods. 
The implication here is that the leader¬ 
ship orientation of the camp director 
and senior staff are very important to 
the morale and work relations of camp. 
Actions speak louder than words, and 
their supervisory behaviour may deter¬ 
mine more of what their staff do than 
they suspect. Group-centered leader¬ 
ship cannot flourish in a dominating 
climate established by the senior staff. 

Finally, we can be pretty sure that 
counsellors who use planned or system¬ 
atic methods in working with their 
cabin groups are likely to be more 
effective than counsellors who operate 
on impulses of the group. Systematic 
methods are based on the assumption 
that a thoughtful analysis of the group’s 
situation (backed up where possible 
with objective measurements) that 
leads to some experimental action plan 
that will be tried out and evaluated is 
the application of the scientific method 
to group work. 

Let us then add to our previous six 
criteria of effective camp counsellors 
the following: 

7. ability to share leadership with 
campers (does not dominate group 
and make them dependent on 
him) 

8. able to help campers make their 
own decisions, plan their own pro¬ 
gramme, etc. 

9. can use systematic group work 
methods and benefit from training 
and supervision in these methods. 

The Tenth Criterion of Effective 
Camp Leadership 

Now there is one very important 
criterion of effective camp leadership 
that must be added to complete the 
list of ten. I have left it ’till last as 
most of you know very well what it is. 
It is, of course, knowledge and ability 


128 


Canadian Camping 


in camp-related skills. A leader may 
have all of the above nine criteria but 
until he has the tenth he is not fully 
able to utilize his potentialities nor the 
potentialities of our wonderful camp 
settings. The would-be camp leader 
needs a certain minimum repertoire of 
camp skills—enough to enable him to 
relax and feel comfortable in a rugged, 
out-of-doors camp setting and to help 
campers develop similar competence in 
a camp setting which leads to security, 
confidence and recognition. In sum¬ 
mary, then, camp staff need to be com¬ 
patible with camp life and technically 
competent in camping skills. 

10. compatible with camp life and 
technically competent in camping 
skills. 

Other Camp Research 

In the past few years my colleagues 
and I have done considerable research 
in identifying characteristics of success¬ 
ful camp and agency leaders (to im¬ 
prove selection), using these character¬ 
istics as the focus of training pro¬ 
grammes, and then measuring change 
toward these characteristics. 

Out of some fifteen areas of attitude 
or behaviour we found four that cor¬ 
related significantly with success on the 
job. These were group-centered leader¬ 
ship attitudes, non-authoritarian beliefs, 
flexible as opposed to rigid attitudes, 
and a friendly or accepting orientation 
to others. Counsellors who ranked high 
on these qualities tended to be identi¬ 
fied most frequently by senior staff as 
the best counsellors. Training pro¬ 
grammes in camp, in Sir George 
Williams University classes, and in 
training laboratories have been con¬ 
ducted focusing on these attitudes and 
behaviours as training goals. Most of 
these programmes have significantly 
modified or developed these character¬ 
istics in the desired direction. We now 
have a fairly extensive body of know¬ 
ledge on some of the factors in training

Situated in the beautiful Haliburton

Applications are invited for placement 
of boys and girls between the ages of 
4 and 17 who are showing severe 
emotional disturbance or mental ill¬ 
ness, for short-term, intensive indivi¬ 
dual and group treatment and 
diagnostic assessement in selected 
small groups, under the direction of 
professionally trained and skilled staff. 
Camp operates from July 3 to August 
28, 1964. Fee—$1200.00, all costs 
included.

No Fishiny Here 

FOREST 

FIRE 

LAST YEAR 


The ideal holiday . . . camping and fishing . . . can be spoiled by a forest fire. 
The loss of forest cover makes cool waters run warm and fill with sediment. Since 
this ruins fishing, the responsible camper is careful to take the common-sense 
precautions which prevent forest fire.
